title: Down the Well to the Meadow
text:
Once upon a time a man and a woman married, and each of them brought a daughter into the house. The wife’s daughter was lazy and slow and never lifted a finger. The man’s daughter was quick and willing, but it made no difference. Whatever she did, she could never please her stepmother, and both the wife and her daughter would have been glad to be rid of her.

One day the two girls were sent to sit by the well and spin. The wife’s daughter was given fine, soft flax. The man’s daughter got nothing but bristles, stiff pig’s bristles that will hardly spin at all.

“Oh, you’re always so quick and so clever,” said the wife’s daughter. “But I’m not afraid to race you at spinning, all the same.”

So they agreed: whoever’s thread broke first would go down the well.

It wasn’t long before the man’s daughter’s thread snapped. And so down the well she had to go.

But when she reached the bottom, she hadn’t so much as a bruise. She got to her feet and looked around. Behind her, the well was nothing but a dark stone arch in a grassy bank. In front of her, a green meadow stretched as far as she could see.

She walked a little way across the meadow and came to a fence woven of brushwood. She had to get over it.

“Oh, don’t tread hard on me,” said the fence, “and I’ll help you another day.”

So she made herself as light as a feather and stepped so carefully that she hardly touched it.

A little farther on she met a big brindled cow with a wooden milking bowl hanging from her horns. Her udder was so full and round that it almost brushed the grass.

“Oh, please milk me,” said the cow. “I’m fit to burst. Drink as much as you like, and pour the rest over my hooves, and I’ll help you another day.”

The man’s daughter did as the cow asked. The moment she touched the teats, the milk came squirting into the bowl. She drank until she wasn’t thirsty any more, poured the rest over the cow’s hooves and hung the bowl back on her horns.

After a while she met a ram. His wool was so long and thick that it dragged along the ground behind him, and a great pair of shears hung from one of his horns.

“Oh, shear me,” said the ram. “Here I go, dragging all this wool about, puffing and panting, and it’s so hot I’m fit to choke. Take as much as you want, and wind the rest round my neck, and I’ll help you another day.”

She was glad to. The ram climbed into her lap of his own accord and lay as still as a stone, and she sheared him so neatly that he didn’t get so much as a scratch. She took as much wool as she wanted and wound the rest round his neck.

Then she came to an apple tree so loaded with apples that every branch was bowed to the ground. A little pole leaned against the trunk.

“Oh, please pick my apples,” said the apple tree, “so my branches can straighten up. It’s hard, standing crooked like this. But knock them down gently, so you don’t hurt me. Eat as many as you like, and lay the rest by my roots, and I’ll help you another day.”

She picked all the apples she could reach, and then she took the pole and knocked the rest down, carefully. She ate till she was full and laid the rest neatly by the roots.
imagePrompt: The Man’s Daughter, a clever, hardworking stepdaughter with a gentle expression, lands unharmed at the bottom of a deep well and rises to her feet in a lovely green meadow. She looks around in wonder at the bright grass and wildflowers spreading far and wide, the dark stone well-mouth behind her like a doorway from the world above, as soft sunlight washes the meadow in calm, storybook light.

title: The Blue Chest
text:
Then she walked a long, long way, until she came to a big farm. A troll-wife lived there with her daughter. The girl went in and asked if they needed a maid.

“Oh, it’s no use,” said the troll-wife. “We’ve had plenty of girls, and not one of them was any good.”

But the girl asked so nicely that they took her on all the same. And the first thing the troll-wife did was hand her a sieve and tell her to fetch water in it.

The girl thought this rather unreasonable. But she went. When she came to the well, the little birds were perched on its rim, and they sang:

“Smear with clay, stick with straw! Smear with clay, stick with straw!”

So she did. She smeared clay over the sieve and stuck straw in the holes, and after that she could carry water in it as well as in any bucket. But when she brought it in, the troll-wife took the sieve and turned it this way and that.

“You never thought of that yourself!” she said.

Then she was sent to the cowshed to muck it out and do the milking. The shovel in there was so big and heavy that she couldn’t manage it. She couldn’t even lift it, and she had no idea what to do. But the birds sang that she should take the broom handle and toss out a little, and the rest would fly after. She did, and before she knew it the cowshed was as clean as if it had been both mucked out and swept.

Next came the milking. But the cows were so restless, kicking and stamping, that she couldn’t get near them. From outside the window the birds sang:

“A little squirt, a little sup, for little birds to drink it up!”

So she squirted a thin stream of milk out to the birds, and at once the cows stood still and let themselves be milked. They didn’t kick, they didn’t stamp, and they didn’t lift so much as a hoof.

When she came in with the milk, the troll-wife said, “You never thought of that yourself! But now you can take this black wool and wash it white.”

How was she to do that? She had never seen anyone wash black wool white. But she didn’t say a word. She took the wool out to the well, and there the little birds sang that she should put it in the big tub that stood there, and it would come out white. And white it came.

“No, no!” said the troll-wife when she came in with the wool. “There’s no use keeping you. You can do anything. In the end you’ll vex the life out of me. You’d better take your wages and go.”

Then she set out three chests in a row: one red, one green and one blue. The girl could have any one of them, and that would be her wages. She didn’t know which to choose. But the little birds came fluttering in at the window, singing:

“Don’t take the green, don’t take the red, but take the blue we’ve marked for you with crosses three upon the lid!”

So she took the blue one, just as the birds had sung. The troll-wife’s face went hard as stone.

“Curse you!” she said. “You’ll pay for this.”

As the man’s daughter was leaving, the troll-wife hurled a red-hot iron bar after her. But the girl sprang behind the door and hid, and the bar missed her. The little birds had told her what to do.
imagePrompt: Inside the Troll-Wife’s remote farmhouse, The Troll-Wife—a harsh mistress—stands rigidly beside three chests set in a row: one red, one green, and one blue marked with three crosses on top. The Man’s Daughter reaches out and firmly takes the blue chest as her wages, while small Singing Birds hover nearby as if guiding her choice, and the troll-wife’s face tightens with anger at the selection.

title: Treasure in the Pigsty
text:
She walked as fast as her legs would carry her. But when she reached the apple tree, she heard a rumbling on the road behind her. It was the troll-wife and her daughter, coming after her. The girl was so frightened she didn’t know where to turn.

“Come here to me,” said the apple tree, “and I’ll help you. Creep in under my branches and hide. If they catch you, they’ll take the chest from you and tear you to pieces.”

She did, and before long the troll-wife and her daughter came rushing up.

“Have you seen a girl go by here?” said the troll-wife.

“Oh yes,” said the apple tree. “One ran past a while ago. But she’s so far off by now that you’ll never catch her.”

So the troll-wife turned round and went home.

The girl went on. But when she reached the ram, she heard the rumbling on the road again, and she knew the troll-wife had changed her mind.

“Come here to me,” said the ram, “and I’ll help you. Hide under my wool, and they won’t see you. Otherwise they’ll take the chest from you and tear you to pieces.”

She crept in under the wool she had wound round his neck herself, and along came the troll-wife, tearing up the road.

“Have you seen a girl go by here?” she asked the ram.

“Oh yes,” said the ram. “I saw one a while ago. But she ran so fast you’ll never catch her.”

So the troll-wife turned round and went home.

When the girl had got as far as the cow, she heard the rumbling yet again.

“Come here to me,” said the cow, “and I’ll help you. Hide under my udder. Otherwise the troll-wife will come and take the chest from you and tear you to pieces.”

It wasn’t long before she came.

“Have you seen a girl go by here?” the troll-wife asked the cow.

“Yes, I saw one a while ago,” said the cow. “But she’s far away now, she ran so fast. You won’t catch her.”

So the troll-wife turned round and went home.

The girl walked on and on. She was nearly back at the brushwood fence when she heard the rumbling on the road once more, and now she was truly afraid, for she knew the troll-wife had turned back one more time.

“Come here to me,” said the fence, “and I’ll help you. Crawl in under my twigs so they can’t see you. Otherwise they’ll take the chest from you and tear you to pieces.”

She scrambled in under the twigs.

“Have you seen a girl go by here?” the troll-wife asked the fence.

“No, I haven’t seen any girl,” said the fence. And it grew so angry that it spat and crackled, and it made itself so big and tall that there was no getting over it. There was nothing the troll-wife could do but turn round and go home.

When the man’s daughter came home safe and sound, her stepmother and stepsister were more jealous of her than ever. For now she was lovelier than before, and so fine that it was a joy to look at her. They wouldn’t have her in the house. They drove her out to the pigsty, and there she had to live.

She scrubbed the pigsty until it was clean and tidy. Then she opened the chest to see what wages she had been paid. The moment she lifted the lid, out came so much gold and silver and so many lovely things that the walls and the roof were hung with them from end to end, and the pigsty was finer than the grandest king’s palace.

When her stepmother and stepsister saw that, they were beside themselves, and they began asking what her place had been like.

“Oh,” said the man’s daughter, “you can guess, since I got wages like these. Such people, and such a mistress! You won’t find their like anywhere.”
imagePrompt: In a scrubbed, tidy pigsty turned radiant, The Man’s Daughter lifts the lid of the blue chest and a dazzling heap of gold, silver, and lovely things spills upward in glittering abundance. The humble wooden walls and roof seem hung with shining riches, transforming the pigsty into something finer than a king’s hall, while her gentle, astonished smile reflects the warm glow of her reward.

title: The Red Chest
text:
Now the wife’s daughter was set on going into service too, so that she could get a chest of gold like that. They sat down to spin again, but this time the wife’s daughter got the bristles and the man’s daughter the flax, and whoever’s thread broke first would go down the well. It wasn’t long before the wife’s daughter’s thread broke, as you might guess, and so they threw her down the well.

It went the same way with her. She fell to the bottom without a bruise and landed in a lovely green meadow. When she had walked a little way, she came to the fence.

“Don’t tread hard on me,” said the fence, “and I’ll help you another day.”

“What do I care about a heap of sticks?” said the wife’s daughter, and she made herself heavy and stamped across the fence till it creaked and cracked.

Soon she came to the cow, heavy with milk.

“Please milk me,” said the cow, “and I’ll help you another day. Drink as much as you like, but pour the rest over my hooves.”

She milked the cow and drank as long as she could, and then there was nothing left for the hooves. She flung the bowl away down the hillside and walked on.

A little farther on she came to the ram, dragging his wool behind him.

“Oh, please shear me,” said the ram, “and I’ll do you a good turn some day. Take as much wool as you like, but wind the rest round my neck.”

She did it, but she went at it so carelessly that she cut great holes in his skin, and she took all the wool for herself.

A little while later she came to the apple tree, bent crooked under its apples.

“Please pick my apples,” said the apple tree, “so my branches can straighten up. But be careful. Eat as many as you like, and lay the rest neatly by my roots, and I’ll help you another day.”

She picked the nearest ones and knocked down the rest with the pole. But she didn’t care what she did. She tore down great branches, ate until she couldn’t swallow another bite and threw the rest under the tree.

Not long after, she came to the farm where the troll-wife lived, and asked for a place there.

“I don’t want any more maids,” said the troll-wife. “Either they’re good for nothing, or they’re too clever by half and cheat me out of what’s mine.”

“I want a place,” said the wife’s daughter, and she wouldn’t give up. At last the troll-wife said she could stay, if she was any good.

The first thing she had to do was fetch water in the sieve. She went to the well and poured water into it, but it ran out as fast as she poured it in. Then the little birds sang:

“Smear with clay, stick with straw! Smear with clay, stick with straw!”

But she didn’t care about their singing. She threw clay at the birds until they flew far away, and then she had to go home with an empty sieve. There the troll-wife gave her a thrashing.

Next she was to muck out the cowshed and do the milking. Muck out a cowshed! She thought she was much too fine for that. She went all the same, but she couldn’t manage the shovel at all, it was so big. The birds told her what they had told the man’s daughter: take the broom handle and toss out a little, and the rest will fly after. But she took the broom and threw it at the birds.

When she came to milk, the cows were so restless that they kicked and stamped, and every time she had a little milk in the bowl, they knocked it over. The birds sang:

“A little squirt, a little sup, for little birds to drink it up!”

But she beat and whacked the cows, and threw everything she could lay her hands on at the birds, and carried on so badly that it was a disgrace. She neither mucked out nor milked. When she came in, the troll-wife gave her a beating and a scolding both. Then she was to wash the black wool white, and that went no better.

Now the troll-wife had had enough. She set out the three chests, one red, one green and one blue, and said she had no use for such a girl, for she was good for nothing. But for wages she could have whichever chest she liked. Then the birds sang:

“Don’t take the green, don’t take the red, but take the blue we’ve marked for you with crosses three upon the lid!”

She didn’t care what the birds sang. She took the red one, because it glowed the most.

Then she set off for home, and she walked in peace and quiet. Nobody came after her.

When she got home, her mother was overjoyed. They carried the chest straight into the best room and set it down in the middle of the floor, for they thought it was full of gold and silver, and that now the walls and the ceiling would be gilded too. The wife’s daughter flung back the lid, grinning. The grin didn’t last. Out poured nothing but worms and toads, heaps of them, crawling and hopping all over the floor.

And every time the wife’s daughter opened her mouth, it was the same: out tumbled worms and toads and every creeping thing you can think of, until at last nobody could bear to be in the same house with her.

And those were the wages she earned in the troll-wife’s service.
imagePrompt: In the great room at home, The Wife’s Daughter—lazy and selfish—throws open the red chest with eager hands, but instead of treasure, a revolting flood of worms and toads pours out onto the floor in writhing heaps. Her face twists from triumph to horror as the crawling horrors spread, the room’s hopeful atmosphere collapsing into disgust and dread.
